title: Rebuilding Jawed.co.in
description: A look at the rebuild of Jawed.co.in from a legacy personal website into a modern, mobile-first site for work, notes, blog, tools and resources.

Rebuilding Jawed.co.in

How I moved an old personal website to a simpler, modern foundation built around the work I do today and the topics I want to document next.

Published: 2026-09-27 · Updated: 2026-10-12

Why rebuild?

Jawed.co.in started as a personal website during the early part of my IT career. It grew around technical certification study material, useful references and a collection of other content. Over the years, much of that technology and many of those pages became outdated.

Instead of trying to modernize every old page, I chose to audit the site, recover useful personal history and rebuild the public structure from scratch.

What changed?

  • The old fixed-layout pages and legacy runtime dependencies were removed.
  • Obsolete certification and technology collections were retired rather than carried forward.
  • The new site uses a small, mobile-first HTML, CSS and JavaScript foundation.
  • Work, Notes, Blog, Tools and Resources now provide the main structure for future content.
  • GitHub is the source of truth and Cloudflare Pages handles deployment.

What I kept

The rebuild keeps the useful part of the site's history: who I am, my career journey, why the site was started and the professional direction I am working in today.

What comes next

The new foundation is intentionally small. I plan to add technical notes, practical tools, useful resources and longer-form posts as there is material worth publishing. The goal is to grow the site through useful content rather than simply recreating the size of the old site.

Start with the job the site needs to do

A rebuild is easier to scope when the site has a clear purpose. I treated this as a professional portfolio and practical knowledge resource, not a general-purpose publishing platform. The primary visitor needs are to understand my work, find useful technical notes, use a small set of practical tools, and locate relevant references.

That purpose shaped the main sections: Work for professional context and evidence; Notes for reusable explanations and workflows; Tools for interactive utilities; Resources for links to primary documentation; and Blog for longer-form project and learning write-ups. A page belongs only when it serves a clear visitor task.

Choose a small technical foundation

The published site uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript with GitHub as the source of truth and Cloudflare Pages for deployment. This keeps ordinary content pages straightforward to inspect and avoids requiring a large application runtime for every visit.

  • Static pages for reading: most profile, note, blog and resource content can be delivered as ordinary HTML.
  • JavaScript where it adds a clear function: search filters and browser-based utilities use scripts for specific interactions rather than making every page depend on a large client-side application.
  • Separate interactive boundaries: tools and AI experiences are treated differently from editorial pages because they have different privacy, reliability, and user-expectation considerations.
  • Explicit source and deployment: changes are committed to version control, reviewed in a bounded pull request, and then deployed from the main branch.

A smaller stack is not automatically better for every site. Here, it fits a content-led portfolio where most pages do not need server-side personalization.

Retire outdated material instead of preserving it blindly

Legacy content can contain useful history, but old pages can also create confusing navigation, duplicate topics, obsolete instructions and maintenance work. I chose to preserve the professional story and the material that could be made useful, rather than copying every old page into the new structure.

For each content area, the useful questions were: is it still accurate, does it serve a current visitor need, can it be maintained, and does it belong on this public site? If the answer was no, retiring the page was better than keeping it only for volume.

Make quality checks part of publishing

For a multi-page static site, one successful homepage check is not enough. A broken internal link, missing sitemap entry, stale metadata or a page that is omitted from navigation can remain hidden unless the site is checked as a whole.

  • Content and route integrity: published pages should have a valid source file, a unique route and an appropriate sitemap entry.
  • Navigation and internal links: related notes should help readers continue a task without creating dead ends or misleading paths.
  • Metadata and structured data: titles, descriptions, canonical URLs and structured data should agree with the visible page.
  • Accessibility and responsive behavior: labels, keyboard interaction, focus states and narrow-screen layouts should be checked alongside desktop presentation.
  • Security and performance: keep scripts and third-party behavior deliberate, avoid unnecessary blocking work, and verify the site's security headers and loading safeguards.
  • Deployment verification: check the production deployment and key routes after a change, not just the local source or pull-request preview.

Automated checks catch repeatable defects, but they do not judge whether an article is genuinely useful. Editorial review and technical validation solve different problems and both are necessary.

SEO is a discovery system, not a substitute for useful content

Canonical URLs, a sitemap, descriptive metadata and structured data help search engines interpret a site. They do not make a shallow page valuable. The content still needs to answer a real question, explain its scope, and provide a useful next step.

I also treat navigation as part of discovery: related notes point to one another where the relationship is real, topic pages group material by visitor intent, and resources link to primary documentation rather than reproducing large portions of third-party material.

Lessons from the rebuild

  • Define boundaries before adding features. Separate editorial content, interactive tools and AI surfaces so their responsibilities and risks remain clear.
  • Prefer maintainable content over page count. A smaller set of accurate, distinct pages is more useful than a large collection of near-duplicates.
  • Automate objective checks. Link, route, metadata and configuration checks should be repeatable and run during review.
  • Keep examples honest. Professional work examples must be sanitized and should not imply access to employer systems or disclose confidential details.
  • Verify the deployed result. Source code and preview checks are necessary, but production deployment status and user-facing behavior are the final operational checks.
  • Keep improving from evidence. Search data, visitor feedback, broken-link reports and review findings should inform the next change instead of adding features without a clear need.

title: How to Triage a Workplace App Access Issue
description: An illustrative IT support walkthrough for scoping app access issues, testing assumptions safely, validating fixes and preparing useful escalations.

How to Triage a Workplace App Access Issue: An Illustrative Walkthrough

A step-by-step example of how to scope an application access problem, separate observations from assumptions, choose safe checks and prepare a useful handoff.

October 2026 · Illustrative scenario

First, define the problem

This is a fictional teaching scenario, not a report of an actual user incident. Imagine a user says, “The workplace scheduling app will not open.” That sentence describes a symptom, but it does not yet tell us whether the cause is the device, account, network, application or service.

The first step is to clarify the task and impact:

  • What exact action fails: opening the app, signing in, loading a page or completing a particular operation?
  • What does the user see? Capture the exact user-visible message without copying secrets or unnecessary personal information.
  • When did it start, and is it repeatable or intermittent?
  • Can the user complete other required tasks, and is anyone else affected?

Step 1: Establish the scope

Use the smallest safe comparisons available. Do not ask for passwords or authentication codes, and do not access another person's account without authorization.

  • User scope: does the problem appear limited to one user, or have multiple authorized users reported it?
  • Device scope: does the symptom occur on this device only, or is an approved comparison available?
  • Application scope: do other applications work as expected, or is the wider device experience affected?
  • Service scope: is there a known service incident or a shared dependency that the support team can check?

These comparisons narrow the next question; they do not prove the root cause by themselves.

Interpret scope comparisons without overclaiming

Use the pattern to choose the next approved check, not to declare a cause. A comparison is useful only when the conditions are relevant and the test is authorized.

Observed patternReasonable next questionWhat it does not prove
One user reports the issue; others have not reported it.Does the user's role, access, session or workflow differ in a relevant way?It does not establish that the account is faulty; the issue may be intermittent or underreported.
The same user can complete the task on an approved comparison device.What differs between the affected and comparison device, such as supported configuration or application state?It does not by itself prove a hardware defect or justify removing management controls.
Multiple users report the same symptom.Is there a shared application, identity, network or service dependency to verify?It does not confirm an outage until a trusted status source or service owner provides evidence.
Other approved applications work, but one application fails.Does the failing workflow rely on a separate permission, identity path or service dependency?It does not prove the entire network is healthy or rule out a partial dependency failure.
An approved status channel reports a matching incident.Does the reported incident match the affected service, time and observed symptom?It does not prove that every user's issue has the same cause; record the match and remaining uncertainty.

Decision rule: state the observation first, identify the next question it raises, and keep the cause as a hypothesis until suitable evidence confirms it. Do not test another person's account or make a cross-device comparison unless policy and authorization explicitly permit it.

Step 2: Record evidence before changing anything

Suppose the user can reach other approved services, but the scheduling app displays an access error. Record that as an observation. Do not immediately conclude that the network is healthy or that the user's account is broken: the application may depend on separate identity, DNS, VPN, authorization or service components.

A useful evidence record could include:

  • the affected task and exact error text;
  • approximate time and whether the failure repeats;
  • application and operating-system context when relevant;
  • which approved comparisons were performed and their results;
  • recent relevant changes, clearly marked as context rather than confirmed cause.

Only record checks that were actually performed. Do not manufacture results to make a ticket appear complete.

Step 3: Choose one discriminating check

Pick a check that can distinguish between plausible explanations and is permitted by your support role. For example, confirm whether an approved service-status channel reports an incident, or ask the service-owning team to verify whether the observed error matches a known access problem.

A good check has a clear question and an interpretable result. Avoid changing several settings at once, disabling security controls, bypassing VPN or access policy, removing device management, or repeatedly reinstalling software without evidence.

If the next step needs elevated privileges, affects shared infrastructure, risks data loss or falls outside the documented procedure, stop and escalate instead of experimenting.

Step 4: Separate facts from hypotheses

Keep the investigation language precise:

  • Observed: the app shows a particular access error at the recorded time.
  • Tested: other approved services worked on the same device; the result was recorded.
  • Possible: an application-specific identity or service dependency may be involved.
  • Confirmed: use this label only when appropriate evidence establishes the cause.

If a service owner later confirms an outage, update the ticket with that evidence. Until then, “possible service-side issue” is more accurate than stating that the service is definitely the cause.

Step 5: Validate the original task

After an approved fix or confirmed service recovery, have the user repeat the original task. “The error disappeared” is not enough if the user still cannot complete the workflow.

  • Repeat the same action that originally failed.
  • Confirm the expected result with the user or an approved test.
  • Check whether any related symptom remains.
  • Record the action, result and any follow-up that is still needed.

Step 6: Make the handoff actionable

If another team must continue, the handoff should let them start from the current state rather than repeat the entire investigation. Include the symptom and impact, scope comparisons, relevant timestamps, checks and results, changes already made, what remains uncertain, and the specific question or action requested.

Keep public examples sanitized. Do not publish internal hostnames, access URLs, employee or customer details, screenshots containing private data, credentials, tokens or restricted operational procedures.

The reusable pattern

  1. Define the task and user impact.
  2. Scope the issue across user, device, application and service.
  3. Collect observations and test results.
  4. Choose one safe check that can distinguish likely explanations.
  5. Keep facts separate from hypotheses.
  6. Validate the original workflow after a supported change.
  7. Document the current state and escalate with a clear next step.

This pattern complements the Service Desk troubleshooting workflow, user/device/service scoping guide and ticket documentation guide.

Limits of this example

Real incidents vary by product, identity model, network design, organization policy and user impact. This walkthrough is a reasoning framework, not a diagnosis or a replacement for vendor documentation, service status information, approved internal procedures or specialist escalation.
